title: A Mother's Purification After Childbirth
overview: This chapter sets out how long a new mother stays away from holy places after giving birth and what offerings mark her return to full worship.

parts.label: After a son is born (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Bleeding after birth made a mother ritually "unclean", a temporary status that kept her from holy places and sacred food, much as during her monthly period. She stayed closely apart for seven days, her son was circumcised on the eighth day, and she then waited 33 more days before returning to the sanctuary.

parts.label: After a daughter is born (v. 5)
parts.note: Both waiting periods are doubled, making 80 days in all instead of 40. The text gives no reason, and readers and scholars have long been unsure why.

parts.label: Offerings that end the wait (vv. 6-7)
parts.note: When the days were over, she brought a year-old lamb to be burned whole as a gift to God, and a pigeon or dove for what is often called a "sin offering". Many scholars think "purification offering" is a better name, reading it as a rite that restored her ritual status so she could take full part in worship again, though older interpreters often linked it to human sinfulness.

parts.label: A gentler rule for the poor (v. 8)
parts.note: A family that could not afford a lamb could bring two birds instead, so cost did not keep anyone from being restored. The Gospel of Luke says Mary brought this two-bird offering after Jesus was born, suggesting his family was poor.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether this uncleanness was meant to picture humanity's inborn sinfulness, as many older interpreters held, or was mainly about blood, life and the boundary between ordinary life and the holy, with no moral meaning at all.
think: Why do you think so many cultures, ancient and modern, surround childbirth with rituals of rest, separation and return?
